summary: Argues that the Data Transfer and File Transfer Protocols could be revised and simplified based on implementation experience, TIP capabilities and Datacomputer needs. It suggests specific changes to prompt discussion at the upcoming workshop.

plainLanguage.summary: After trying data and file transfer methods, the author proposes changes to make them easier to use and implement. The paper collects ideas for discussion rather than setting a final design.

subtitle: A discussion paper proposing simplifications to the Data Transfer and File Transfer Protocols.

tldr.problem: Implementation experience exposed difficulties for TIP users and other services in the proposed Data Transfer Protocol and File Transfer Protocol.
tldr.mechanism: The author discusses simpler DTP modes, printable FTP commands, flexible data formats, separate data connections, and a way to restart transfers.
tldr.outcome: RFC 310 is intended to prompt discussion at a forthcoming workshop. It updates RFCs 264 and 265.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 310 as Unknown and records that it updates RFCs 264 and 265. It is a discussion paper about possible changes to early transfer protocols.

sections.title: Experience with Existing Transfers
sections.content:
The author describes several ways sites were already moving files, including TENEX CPYNET and file transfer over modified TELNET programs. CPYNET can choose a byte size suited to the computer, while TELNET-based file sending processes each character and can be slower.

These experiences, along with TIP capabilities and Datacomputer requirements, led the author to ask whether DTP and FTP could be simplified.
sections.plainLanguage: Sites had already found ways to transfer files, but each approach had trade-offs. The author uses those experiences to question whether the proposed protocols are too difficult.

sections.title: Needs of TIPs and Services
sections.content:
The paper says TIPs will not support DTP in its current form, which makes DTP-based services inconvenient for TIP users. It suggests allowing ASCII in DTP and using printable ASCII strings for user-level commands.

It also describes Datacomputer interest in a full-duplex control connection and Remote Job Service needs for a common default data type, agreement on formats, and recovery after transfer failures.
sections.plainLanguage: Small terminals and other network services need simpler ways to issue commands and choose data formats. They also need a way to recover if a transfer fails.

sections.title: Possible Changes to DTP and FTP
sections.content:
For DTP, the author suggests dropping transparent mode, keeping block and indefinite bit-stream modes, and making the modes-available handshake optional. A simplified DTP could handle data format while a higher-level protocol handles errors and recovery.

For FTP, suggestions include printable commands, allowing a user and server to agree on data type and structure, choosing a suitable byte size, and providing a restart method. The paper leaves these choices open for discussion.
sections.plainLanguage: The author proposes fewer transfer modes and commands that people can read. He also wants the two sides to agree on data form and support resuming a failed transfer.
